title: Scale Elemental Analysis of Some Commercially Important Fishes and Their Potential Links to Fish Feeding Patterns and the Natural Environment
content: The article represents scale elemental analysis of three commercially important fishes Cyprinus carpio, Lates calcarifer, and Chrysochir aureus. The concentrations of As, Be, Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Hg, Mn, Ni, Pb, Se, V, and Zn using Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS). It was revealed that fish scale microchemistry differed in connection with their natural environment, habitat, and feeding habits. Higher levels of Be, Co, and Zn in the scales of C. carpio, which is a freshwater fish, are perhaps due to increased bioavailability of the elements, aquatic pollution, and fish’s interaction with sediment. L. calcarifer, collected from the brackish water environment, derived more Cu from mixing-zone chemistry and anthropogenic inputs, as well as from their prey. Marine fish, C. aureus, displayed significantly higher levels of As, Mn, Ni, and Se in their scales, likely due to the complexation process and their inherent seawater abundance. Significantly elevated As, Be, Cd, Co, Mn, Se, and Zn in the scales of benthopelagic fish may stem from prolonged exposure to water column particulates and dietary uptake. Omnivorous fish accumulate significantly higher levels of Be, Co, and Zn than their carnivorous counterpart that which might be attributed to a combination of their broad spectrum diet pattern. Although these differences could be caused by other variables such as species-specific physiology or geographic distribution, the findings suggests that fish scale microchemistry may be linked to trophic ecology and environmental exposure. The study might contribute to the future development of noninvasive approaches utilizing fish scales for ecological and environmental assessment.
